title: JPMorgan CEO Dimon warns customers of ‘liability transfer’ with AI
summary: As Meta’s Muse reignites fears over artificial intelligence-driven deposit flight, Jamie Dimon on Tuesday said bank customers using AI agents need to understand the risks.
excerpt: An article from. JPMorgan CEO Dimon warns customers of ‘liability transfer’ with AI. As Meta’s Muse reignites fears over artificial intelligence-driven deposit flight, Jamie Dimon on Tuesday said bank customers using AI agents need to understand the risks. Published Oct. 13, 2026. Caitlin Mullen Senior Editor. Share Copy link. Email. LinkedIn. X/Twitter. Facebook. Print. License. Add us on Google. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon cautioned customers Tuesday that if they’re giving artificial intelligence agents access to their bank accounts, they’re owning that decision. The comments from the CEO of the biggest U. S. bank come just weeks after Meta’s AI assistant Muse debuted, reigniting conversation around AI-cash sorting concerns for lenders. “You’ve got to make sure customers aren't hurt by it, and so that is of concern,” Dimon said during the bank’s third-quarter earnings call. “You don't want rogue agents, and there could be thousands of them. ”. “If people are using them, they should understand the risk,” the CEO said. “There's a liability transfer. They should understand the liability transfer. If data is being misused, they should understand it’s being misused. ”. “We have to make sure we protect our customer in the right kind of way. So we’re building tools to do that, too,” Dimon said. “In the meantime, we're not going to allow just any outside agent to come in inside the company because it's too risky for the clients and for JPMorgan. ”. Consulting firm McKinsey warned in April that retail banks may face disintermediation of their relationships with customers if AI agents acting on consumers’ behalf move money in pursuit of better rates. For its part, JPMorgan’s AI-powered Smart Cash tool – which moves customer money between accounts at the New York City-based bank to maximize yield and manage cash flow – is in pilot, CFO Jeremy Barnum said Tuesday. “The strategic question is not whether AI pulls deposits out of checking, but who owns the agent, the wallet and ultimately the customer relationship,” Bank of America Securities analyst Ebrahim Poonawala said in a Sept. 23 note. Regulators should also consider how agentic AI’s potential impact on deposits could affect liquidity risk management, Dimon said. “It’s a new world,” and “with all these bots and agents and stuff like that, could someone get hurt and cause a problem? Maybe. If I was a regulator, I’d try to be prepared for that,” Dimon said. Bank executives also faced AI expense-related questions Tuesday, as the industry begins to feel pressure to show return on AI investment while costs have soared. Last year , Dimon said the bank’s annual AI-generated savings of $2 billion roughly equal what it spends yearly on the technology. Asked for updated figures Tuesday, Barnum put the bank’s annual AI spending somewhere closer to $700 million, not $2 billion, but also said that figure is “a little stale at this point. ”. “If you sort of price out the amount of time we're all spending thinking about it, you could probably get a higher number, too,” the CFO said. “It’s, at this point, not really something that you can ring-fence. It's pretty well diffused inside the whole institution, and it's obviously a very, very high priority. ”. As for the benefits, Barnum said he’s trying to move away from quantifying that, in part because the previous estimate would have included more traditional AI and machine learning uses. Generative and agentic AI’s impact on productivity, expenses and revenue “is the more relevant focus right now, and I'm just very reluctant to spend a lot of energy quantifying it because it winds up wasting a lot of people's time inside the institution, when we actually need to get them to focus on doing things,” Barnum said. AI benefits aren’t yet observable in JPMorgan’s quarterly earnings, the CFO said. “As important and dramatic and exciting as this theme is, it takes a long time to really do things that are visible in an institution of our size,” he said. title: First UK lender goes live on a sovereign AI platform
excerpt: . Scottish Building Society has become the first UK lender to go live on a sovereign AI platform built specifically for core banking, in partnership with SBS and NVIDIA. The platform runs entirely within the building society's own environment on Amazon Web Services, meaning no customer or mortgage data leaves their walls. The Society says it is already seeing 30 to 40% faster response times with more consistent outputs, while maintaining the full explainability and audit trail that regulators require. SBS says for UK banks and building societies exploring AI, compliance has historically been the blocker. Most AI platforms require customer and mortgage data to leave the institution's environment, creating significant regulatory exposure under FCA and PRA oversight. Scottish Building Society’s deployment of SBS and NVIDIA’s AI system addresses that need, and the platform is now available to other SBS clients across the UK. In the near future, the solution will encompass Agentic AI, which automates core banking workflows with autonomous agents that execute multi-step banking processes, transparently with human oversight and within a fully governed environment. Eric Bierry, CEO of SBS, commented: “Banks want AI they can trust, explain and run wherever their data must live. By building with NVIDIA, we can give our customers that assurance without compromising on governance. We are already seeing the results from this work with our early customers, and we look forward to continuing to roll out these capabilities as we help more financial institutions take advantage of AI efficiencies. ”. Aser Blanco, global head of banking at NVIDIA, added: "SBS is turning a governed AI runtime into a shared intelligence layer beneath its entire banking platform. With NVIDIA, SBS is giving banks the tools they need to deploy generative and agentic AI across cloud and sovereign infrastructure. Once they have this infrastructure in place, the capabilities it unlocks drive efficiency and ultimately power growth. ”.

title: Banking Regulators Step Up AI Scrutiny Over Cyber and Stability Risks
excerpt: . Banking regulators in the US and Europe are increasing scrutiny of AI use, focusing on autonomous agents, cyber risk and dependence on technology providers. SHARE. Banking regulators in the United States and Europe are increasing scrutiny of how banks use advanced artificial intelligence, amid concerns that cyberattacks or poorly controlled AI agents could disrupt financial institutions and, in extreme cases, threaten wider financial stability. Regulators are asking banks how they use powerful AI models, whether autonomous systems can be stopped quickly and how dependent they are on outside technology providers. Three major US banking regulators, including the Federal Reserve, are questioning banks about their use of advanced AI systems. Their questions include whether institutions use Chinese-developed AI technology, whether AI agents are deployed in cyber defence and how much freedom those systems are given to act without human approval. Regulators are also asking whether banks can shut down autonomous systems if they start behaving unexpectedly. That issue matters because an AI agent is different from a normal chatbot. A chatbot mainly responds to a user. An AI agent can be given access to tools and systems, allowing it to perform tasks, make decisions and take multiple actions with less direct human supervision. Inside a bank, such systems could potentially monitor cyber threats, analyse transactions or help manage operational processes. The concern is what happens if an agent makes a serious mistake, is manipulated by an attacker or takes an action that nobody intended. US regulators have not yet announced new binding rules specifically covering these systems. The current focus appears to be on understanding how banks are deploying them and whether existing controls are strong enough. Europe focuses on recovery and dependence on outside providers. European regulators are examining the same problem from another angle. Supervisors including the Bank of England and European Central Bank are pressing institutions to strengthen recovery plans in case AI systems fail or contribute to cyber disruption. Banks increasingly rely on a small number of technology companies for cloud infrastructure, AI models and other critical services. That creates concentration risk. If many major banks depend on the same AI provider and that system experiences a serious failure, the problem may not remain limited to one institution. A disruption could potentially affect several banks at once. Regulators therefore want lenders to understand where their most important AI systems come from, what happens if those services become unavailable and whether they can continue operating without them. The problem is similar to relying on a single supplier for an essential component. If that supplier fails, every customer depending on it can face trouble at the same time. title: Sampath Bank only Sri Lankan Bank recognised for AI Innovation at ICC Emerging Asia Banking Awards
excerpt: . Sampath Bank PLC has received a Special Appreciation Award for AI/ML Implementation in Banking at the ICC Emerging Asia Banking Conclave & Awards 2026 held in New Delhi, India, becoming the only bank in Sri Lanka to receive this recognition while highlighting the Bank’s continued progress in applying Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) to strengthen banking operations, improve customer experiences and support data-driven decision-making. Presented by the Indian Chamber of Commerce (ICC), the regional awards celebrate excellence among financial institutions across the BIMSTEC region, including Sri Lanka, India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Myanmar and Thailand. The AI/ML recognition acknowledges organisations that are successfully integrating emerging technologies to improve performance, enhance operational efficiency and create long-term value. The awards are evaluated by an independent panel of former banking and regulatory leaders, while PwC India served as the Process Reviewer to ensure a transparent assessment process. Commenting on the recognition, Darshin Pathinayake , Chief Business Intelligence Officer of Sampath Bank, said, “We are honoured to receive this Special Appreciation Award for AI/ML Implementation in Banking at the ICC Emerging Asia Banking Conclave & Awards 2026. This recognition reflects our commitment to using data, analytics, Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning to create meaningful value for our customers while strengthening innovation and informed decision-making across the Bank. As banking continues to evolve, these technologies are helping us improve customer engagement, speed and convenience, strengthen operational excellence and enhance risk management. This achievement also recognises the dedication of our teams whose expertise continues to advance our data-driven transformation journey. ”. Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning continue to play an increasingly important role in the Bank’s digital transformation strategy. Technology-enabled insights are helping the Bank better understand customer needs, streamline business processes, strengthen risk management capabilities and deliver more relevant financial solutions. Continued investment in advanced analytics is also enabling greater organisational agility while creating sustainable value for customers, shareholders and other stakeholders. Sampath Bank was represented at the event by Darshin Pathinayake, Chief Business Intelligence Officer, and Kiruparan Balachandran, Principal Data Scientist. Pathinayake also participated as an invited panellist during a leadership discussion on trust, technology and transformation, where banking leaders explored digital transformation, cyber resilience, regulatory developments and collaboration between banks, fintechs and technology partners. The latest regional recognition reflects Sampath Bank’s continued focus on combining technology, data and innovation to build a future-ready banking experience while strengthening its position among Sri Lanka’s leading digitally progressive financial institutions. 2026-10-13.

In the US, the Federal Reserve, Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation are questioning banks about safeguards for agentic AI. title: Banking regulators step up scrutiny of AI risks
excerpt: Banking regulators are stepping up efforts to contain growing AI risks, six people familiar with the matter said, with some pointing to the potential for cyberattacks on banks or rogue agents undermining global financial stability. The regulatory scrutiny, fresh details of which are reported here for the first time, reflects growing recognition that advances in frontier AI may require costly investments in cyber recovery, greater attention to dependencies on external technology providers and in some jurisdictions more formal regulatory guidance, sources said. Three top regulators in the United States, including the Federal Reserve, are quizzing banks about their use of advanced artificial intelligence models, two of the people told Reuters, which adds to prior scrutiny. Questions include whether they deploy Chinese-developed technology, use AI agents in cyber defence and can control increasingly autonomous systems, three of the people said. In Europe, supervisors including the Bank of England and the European Central Bank are pressing banks to improve recovery plans, concerned that rapid advances in AI could cause serious harm and disruption in financial markets sooner than previously feared, three people with knowledge of their thinking said. A senior executive at a large European bank said they too are worried about potentially major damage to banking and financial markets “within six months”. The debate over AI oversight has intensified amid warnings from the industry after recent incidents, with JPMorgan JPM. N CEO Jamie Dimon urging corporate leaders to join a US-focused industry group to address AI risks, Reuters reported. US cybersecurity company CrowdStrike said this month a person in China likely used a Chinese-developed AI agent and Anthropic’s Claude Code in a hack on South Korean banks. Rogue AI agents developed by OpenAI were meanwhile involved in a breach of AI platform Hugging Face, Reuters reported. Anthropic researchers have warned that increasingly powerful AI systems could eventually escape human control and even pose an existential threat, prompting calls for stricter regulation. Banks are competing to adopt agentic AI, which can accomplish tasks with minimal human supervision, while also grappling with the challenges of new models including IT weaknesses flagged by Anthropic’s Mythos tool. “The adoption of AI is often outpacing the ability to put the controls in place,” said Michael Woodbridge, London-based cybersecurity partner at Grant Thornton. US regulators focus on autonomous AI. The US regulatory inquiries centre on how banks use agentic AI in areas such as cybersecurity, focusing on whether AI agents are being used to identify, prioritize and respond to threats. Questions from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and the Fed focus on what limits are placed on systems, how their actions are monitored and approved and whether banks can clearly track and audit AI agent decisions, two of the people said. They are also asking what safeguards exist to prevent agents from exceeding their authority, whether humans remain involved in key decisions and how banks can shut down autonomous systems. The OCC, the Fed and the FDIC declined to comment. Through their questions, regulators are probing more specific issues tied to advanced AI models, including the use of autonomous AI agents, foreign-developed models and new cyber risks, the three people with knowledge of their thinking said. The written and verbal inquiries to large, mid-size and smaller banks show regulators are focusing on vulnerabilities from banks’ use of AI and their preparedness to act, they added. Regulators are still gathering information and are not yet being prescriptive about what lenders should be doing, they said. European banks face pressure to strengthen recovery. excerpt: Wealth management in AI age: will machines replace human adviser?. DR MUHAMMAD WAQAS October 14, 2026 4 min read. --> facebook --> twitter --> whatsup --> linkded --> email MORE (3) Messenger. Whatsapp. -->. The writer is Assistant Professor of DHA Suffa University. He can be reached at Muhammad. waqas@dsu. edu. pk. Artificial intelligence is no longer confined to technology laboratories. It has entered our banks, investment platforms and financial institutions and, increasingly, our personal financial decisions. From analysing markets and preparing financial plans to detecting fraud, AI is rapidly changing how wealth is managed. This raises an obvious question: will it eventually replace the human wealth manager?. Traditionally, wealth management has rested on the relationship between a client and an adviser. The adviser does far more than recommend investments. He or she tries to understand the client's finances, family responsibilities, ambitions, tolerance for risk and long-term priorities. A portfolio that looks optimal on a spreadsheet may be wholly unsuitable for someone who cannot emotionally bear large swings in its value. AI is exceptionally good at the mathematical side of this equation. Modern systems can process vast quantities of financial and economic data in a fraction of the time a human analyst would need, compare investment alternatives and monitor portfolios. They can also automate routine administrative work, freeing professionals to spend more time with clients. Recent industry research from LSEG describes this as a shift from gathering information to interpreting and coordinating insights. For ordinary investors, this could be valuable. Personalised advice has long been expensive, and therefore associated with the wealthy. AI-powered tools could reduce costs and extend financial guidance to people who could never afford it. But accessibility should not be confused with reliability. One of the biggest dangers of AI-based advice is that an answer can sound convincing without being correct. Financial decisions involve uncertainty, incomplete information and changing circumstances. A system may produce a sophisticated-looking recommendation while missing the individual's complete financial picture. Research from MIT Sloan found that AI can offer useful guidance on saving, spending and investing, but that its recommendations vary with the quality of information supplied by the user. The researchers also identified weaknesses in responding to income shocks, rebalancing portfolios and managing retirement drawdown. Investors should think twice before treating a chatbot as a personal financial adviser. Then there is the question of accountability. If a human adviser's recommendation causes a client serious harm, regulatory and professional responsibilities apply. An AI system has no professional responsibility or fiduciary judgment. Responsibility ultimately rests with the institution, adviser or individual who deploys it. That is why human oversight will remain critical. The UK's Financial Conduct Authority, in its 2026 wealth-management research, acknowledges both sides. AI can reduce friction, improve efficiency and help close the advice gap, but the regulator also warns of risks involving fraud, cybersecurity and consumer harm. These concerns are far from theoretical. The more financial institutions rely on interconnected digital systems and third-party technology providers, the graver the consequences of a major technological failure. The Financial Stability Board has recently placed AI-related cyber risk among its principal concerns for financial stability, according to Reuters. Privacy is equally important. Wealth management requires highly sensitive information: income, assets, debts, tax circumstances and often family details.
